name: Serbo-Croatian
note: Written in the Latin alphabet, one of the two the language uses.

alphabet.e: a softer ch, near the t in future
a softer j, near the d in during
v, made with a light contact
a rolled r, and a vowel on its own in prst

units.title: BASICS
units.subtitle: Greeting people, naming who is who, and counting to ten

tips.b: Zdravo is neutral and fits any situation. Ćao is informal and passes between friends, family and people of the same age, and it serves as an informal goodbye as well.

Two words address a listener. Ti is singular and informal, used with friends, family and children. Vi is the plural, and also the polite singular for a stranger or an older person; the verb stays plural with it.

Nouns are masculine, feminine or neuter. A noun ending in a consonant is usually masculine, one ending in -a is usually feminine, and one ending in -o or -e is usually neuter. The gender is listed beside each noun.
The verb ending already names the subject, so ja, ti and mi appear only for emphasis or contrast. Dobro sam on its own means I am well.
eg: I am well, whatever the others are.

tips.b: There is no word for a or the. Žena covers woman, a woman and the woman, and the surrounding sentence supplies which reading is meant.
Molim is the word for please. Used alone after hvala it returns the thanks, and used as a question it asks for something to be repeated.
A form addressed to one person has an informal and a polite variant, and the polite one is identical to the plural: izvoli and izvolite, hvala ti and hvala vam.

phrases.e: Yes, of course, here you are

tips.h: One agrees, two has a gender
tips.b: Jedan changes with its noun: jedan čovek, jedna žena, jedno jutro. Dva has the separate feminine form dve. From tri upward the number itself does not change.
Dva, tri and četiri are followed by a count form ending in -a for masculine and neuter nouns and -e for feminine ones. From pet upward the noun stands in the genitive plural.

units.title: EVERYDAY
units.subtitle: Food, drink, colour and the people of a household

tips.h: The object of a verb changes form
tips.b: A noun that receives the action stands in the accusative. A feminine noun in -a takes -u, while a masculine noun for a thing and every neuter noun keep their basic form.
A noun with no article covers a definite reading, an indefinite one and a partial amount. Jedem hleb is I eat bread, I eat the bread and I am eating some bread.
eg: The bread is on the table.

tips.b: Hoću is the first person of hteti, to want, and what is wanted follows in the accusative: hoću vodu, hoću kafu. Želim is the more formal equivalent and behaves the same way.
Šolja, čaša and flaša name a container and are feminine. What the container holds follows in the genitive, which ends in -e for a feminine noun and -a for a masculine one.

tips.h: Adjectives take the gender of the noun
tips.b: An adjective ends in a consonant before a masculine noun, in -a before a feminine one and in -o before a neuter one. The form listed in a dictionary is the masculine.
Red wine is crno vino, black wine. Crven is kept for the colour of an apple, a flag or a jacket.
Moj, tvoj and naš change with the noun that follows them: moj brat, moja sestra, moje dete. The ending follows the gender of the thing owned, not the gender of the owner.
A noun used to call or address a person takes the vocative. A masculine noun adds -e or -u and a feminine noun in -a takes -o: brate, sine, majko, sestro.

tips.h: Brat and dete have odd plurals
tips.b: Brat has the collective plural braća and dete has deca. Both are formed with a collective ending and both decline as feminine singular nouns.

phrases.e: I have a brother and a sister

units.title: ACTIONS
units.subtitle: The present tense, describing things, asking and denying

tips.b: A present form is the stem plus a personal ending. The first person singular ends in -am, -im or -em, and that vowel runs through the whole set: imam, imaš, ima, imamo, imate, imaju.
eg: I have, you have, he has
I speak, you speak, he speaks
I drink, you drink, he drinks

tips.h: Biti has two sets of forms
tips.b: The present of biti has a short set used in ordinary statements, sam, si, je, smo, ste, su, and a full set used for emphasis and for a one-word answer, jesam, jesi, jeste, jesmo, jeste, jesu. A short form never opens a sentence.
Most infinitives end in -ti. A small closed group ends in -ći: ići, moći, reći, doći. The present stem of that group does not follow from the infinitive and is learned with the verb.

tips.h: The adjective stands before the noun
tips.b: An adjective comes before its noun and agrees with it in gender, number and case: velik grad, velika kuća, veliko selo. After biti it agrees in the same way.
The comparative of most adjectives adds -iji to the stem: nov, noviji; star, stariji. A handful are irregular: dobar, bolji; velik, veći; mali, manji; loš, gori.

tips.h: Two ways to ask a yes-no question
tips.b: A yes-no question either puts da li in front of the statement or moves the verb to the front and follows it with li. Both are standard; da li is the more frequent in speech.
Ko, šta, gde, kada, zašto and kako stand first and need no auxiliary verb. The verb follows, and any short form sits between the two.

phrases.e: How much does this wine cost?

tips.h: Ne goes in front of the verb
tips.b: Negation places ne directly before the verb: ne govorim, ne pijem. Three verbs fuse with it instead of taking it as a separate word: nisam from biti, nemam from imati and neću from hteti.
A negative pronoun or adverb does not replace ne; both appear in the clause. Niko ne zna carries two negatives and means nobody knows, and leaving out ne is ungrammatical.
Nema is the negative counterpart of ima and says that something is not there. What is absent stands in the genitive: nema hleba, nema vode, nema vremena.

units.title: AT HOME
units.subtitle: The rooms of a house, the things in it, clothes and animals

tips.h: U and na for a location
tips.b: To state where something is, u or na is followed by the locative case: u kuhinji, u sobi, na krovu. U covers enclosed places and na open or flat ones, and which of the two a place takes is fixed by the word.
With a verb of motion u and na take the accusative instead of the locative, and the pair of cases marks the difference between a place and a destination.
eg: I am going into the room.
The cat is on the roof.
The cat is going onto the roof.

phrases.e: The cat is in the kitchen
I am going to the bathroom

tips.b: Many one-syllable masculine nouns insert -ov- or -ev- before the plural ending: sto, stolovi; nož, noževi; ključ, ključevi. Longer masculine nouns take plain -i: prozori, kreveti.

tips.h: Na for a surface, u for an inside
tips.b: Na with the locative marks contact with a surface: na stolu, na zidu, na podu. U with the locative marks the inside of something: u ormaru, u sobi, u kući.

phrases.e: The key is on the table
The picture is on the wall

tips.h: Garments that exist only in plural
tips.b: Pantalone, cipele and čarape have no singular and take plural agreement: cipele su nove. A single item is counted with par: par cipela.

tips.h: One verb for wearing and carrying
tips.b: Nositi covers both wearing a garment and carrying an object, and what is worn or carried stands in the accusative. Obući se is the separate verb for the act of getting dressed.

phrases.e: I am wearing a red t-shirt
He is wearing a black coat

tips.b: A masculine noun naming a living being takes the genitive form as its accusative: vidim psa, vidim konja, vidim brata. A masculine noun naming a thing keeps its basic form: vidim sto.
Pas drops the a everywhere outside the nominative singular: psa, psu, psi. The same movable a appears in otac, oca and in adjectives such as dobar, dobra.

phrases.e: I have a dog and a cat
The bird is on the roof
I see a horse in the yard

units.title: TIME
units.subtitle: The days, the months, the clock and the weather

tips.h: Days are written in lower case
tips.b: The names of the days start with a small letter: ponedeljak, utorak, sreda. The week begins on Monday, and nedelja is Sunday.

tips.h: U for a day, -om for a habit
tips.b: A single day on which something happens takes u with the accusative: u ponedeljak, u subotu, u nedelju. A day that recurs takes the instrumental on its own: subotom, nedeljom.

phrases.e: On Saturday I go to town

tips.h: Months take u and the locative
tips.b: The month in which something happens takes u with the locative: u januaru, u martu, u julu. The names are masculine and are written with a small letter.
A date is an ordinal number in the genitive followed by the month in the genitive: prvog januara, petog marta. Spoken dates keep the same two endings.

phrases.e: I go to the seaside in July

tips.b: The hour takes u with the accusative of the number, followed by the count form of sat: u jedan sat, u dva sata, u pet sati. The question is Koliko je sati.

tips.h: Parts of the day as adverbs
tips.b: The nouns for the parts of the day have adverb forms that say when something happens, and these stand alone without a preposition.

phrases.e: In the evening I drink tea

tips.b: A statement about the weather uses a neuter adjective with je and no subject at all: hladno je, toplo je, sunčano je. The verb agrees with nothing.
Rain and snow are stated with padati, to fall, and the noun as subject: pada kiša, pada sneg. The verb before the subject is the ordinary order here.

phrases.e: What is the weather like today?

units.title: GETTING AROUND
units.subtitle: Places in town, giving directions, transport and travel

tips.h: U or na is fixed by the place
tips.b: Some places take u and others take na, and the choice belongs to the word rather than to a rule: u banci, u prodavnici, u školi, na pijaci, na pošti, na stanici.
Where English joins two nouns with of, Serbo-Croatian puts the second noun in the genitive: centar grada, vrata kuće, ulica grada.

phrases.e: The bank is in the town centre
I am going to the market
Where is the nearest post office?

tips.b: A command drops the infinitive ending and adds -i for one person and -ite for several. The -ite form is also the polite command to a single person.
Pored, iza, ispred, blizu and do are followed by the genitive: pored banke, iza crkve, ispred škole, do raskrsnice.

phrases.e: The post office is next to the bank
The museum is behind the church

tips.b: The vehicle taken stands in the instrumental with no preposition. A masculine noun adds -om, or -em after a soft consonant, and a feminine noun in -a takes -om.
Ići covers going on foot and going in general, putovati names a journey, and voziti means to drive a vehicle. The destination follows u or na in the accusative.

phrases.e: I go to work by bus
I am buying a train ticket

tips.b: Most verbs exist in two forms. The imperfective presents an action as ongoing or repeated, the perfective presents it as one completed whole. Putovati is imperfective and otputovati perfective; ići is imperfective and poći perfective.

tips.h: A perfective has no present meaning
tips.b: A perfective verb in the present form does not describe the present moment. It appears after da, after kada and in the future: hoću da stignem, kada stignem.
eg: I want to arrive on time.
When I arrive, I will call you.

phrases.e: We are travelling to the seaside
The train arrives at the station
We are going on holiday in July

units.title: PEOPLE
units.subtitle: Feelings, the body, health and describing a person

tips.h: States are stated in the dative
tips.b: A physical or emotional state uses a neuter adjective with je and the dative of the person affected. The person is not the subject of the sentence.
An adjective ending in -an drops that a before any ending: srećan, srećna, srećno; gladan, gladna, gladno. The masculine singular is the only form that keeps it.
Oko and uvo are neuter in the singular and take the feminine plurals oči and uši. Ruka and noga name the whole arm and the whole leg; šaka and stopalo name the hand and the foot alone.
The owner of a body part goes unstated when it is obvious: perem ruke means I wash my hands. A possessive appears only where the owner would otherwise be in doubt.

phrases.e: I wash my hands every morning

tips.h: Boleti makes the part the subject
tips.b: With boleti the aching part is the subject and the person is the object in the accusative: boli me glava, bole me zubi. The verb agrees with the body part, so a plural part takes bole.
Kod with the genitive names the place of a person, and it covers both being there and going there: kod lekara, kod brata, kod kuće.

phrases.e: I am going to the doctor

tips.b: What something is compared against follows od in the genitive: viši od mene, stariji od brata. Nego with the nominative is the alternative construction: viši nego ja.
The superlative is the comparative with naj- written in front of it as one word: najviši, najstariji, najbolji. The group compared within follows u with the locative.

units.title: WORK AND SCHOOL
units.subtitle: School, work, numbers past ten and handling money

tips.b: Mnogo, malo, nekoliko and dosta are followed by the genitive plural, and the quantity word itself never changes: mnogo knjiga, nekoliko dana. An uncountable noun takes the genitive singular: malo vremena.
A feminine noun in -a ends in -i in the locative: škola, u školi; soba, u sobi. A k, g or h in front of that ending softens to c, z or s: knjiga, u knjizi.

phrases.e: I study at school every day
Tomorrow we have an important exam

tips.h: Short forms stand in second place
tips.b: The short forms je, sam, se, mi, te and li occupy the second slot of the clause, straight after the first stressed word or phrase. The rest of the order is free, and whatever stands first carries the emphasis.
eg: It is my father who is the engineer.

tips.b: Most job nouns are masculine and build a feminine with -ica or -ka: konobar, konobarica; prodavac, prodavačica; lekar, lekarka. The masculine also serves as the general term for the occupation.

phrases.e: I work in a big office
She is looking for a new job

tips.h: Tens and units stay separate words
tips.b: A compound number names the ten and then the unit as two separate words, with no linking word between them: dvadeset jedan, trideset pet, sto dvadeset.

tips.h: The last digit governs the noun
tips.b: A compound number governs its noun by the final digit alone. A number ending in one takes the nominative singular, one ending in two, three or four takes the count form, and every other ending takes the genitive plural.

phrases.e: My grandmother is eighty years old
The book has a hundred pages

tips.b: A currency after two, three or four takes the count form, and after five and above the genitive plural: dva dinara, pet dinara, sto evra. The singular stands only after one.

tips.h: The means of payment is instrumental
tips.b: What a sum is paid with stands in the instrumental with no preposition: plaćam karticom, plaćam gotovinom. The ending is the same one that marks a vehicle in autobusom.

phrases.e: I pay by card, not in cash

units.title: OUT AND ABOUT
units.subtitle: Ordering a meal, shopping, pastimes and sport

tips.b: After želim, hoću and mogu the second verb usually appears as da with a present form that agrees with the same subject: želim da naručim. A bare infinitive is also correct and sounds more formal.
Bih with the past participle forms the conditional, which softens a request. The participle agrees in gender with the speaker.
eg: I would like a coffee. (man speaking)
I would like a coffee. (woman speaking)

phrases.e: I would like to order a dish
We have a reservation for two

tips.b: Three demonstratives mark distance. Ovaj points to what is near the speaker, taj to what is near the listener and onaj to what is away from both. Each agrees with its noun: ovaj kaput, ova majica, ovo jelo.
Kupiti and prodati are perfective and name the completed act. Kupovati and prodavati are the imperfective partners, used for a repeated or ongoing one.

phrases.e: I want to buy a jacket
Do you have a larger size?

tips.b: Svirati is used for a musical instrument and igrati for a game or a dance. Both take the accusative: sviram gitaru, igram fudbal.

tips.h: Voleti with da or with a noun
tips.b: A liked activity follows voleti as da with a present form: volim da čitam, volim da slušam muziku. A liked thing follows as a plain accusative: volim muziku.

phrases.e: He plays the guitar in the evening
We watch a movie every Saturday

tips.b: A group of verbs carries the particle se, which follows the same rules as the other short forms and stands in second place: bavim se sportom, zovem se Ana. Se has no meaning of its own in these verbs.
The activity pursued follows baviti se in the instrumental: bavim se plivanjem, bavi se košarkom. Igrati takes the accusative instead: igram košarku.

units.title: THE WORLD
units.subtitle: Nature, the city, countries and further everyday verbs

tips.b: Some nouns have a collective form in -će or -je that names a mass rather than a count: drvo, drveće; cvet, cveće; list, lišće. A collective is neuter singular and takes a singular verb.

tips.h: Neuter nouns that grow a syllable
tips.b: A group of neuter nouns adds -en- or -et- outside the nominative: ime, imena; vreme, vremena; dete, deteta. The added syllable appears in every other case and in the plural.

phrases.e: There are many trees in the forest
The river is cold and deep
The stars are in the sky

tips.b: Pored, kod, preko, iza, ispred and blizu are followed by the genitive: pored zgrade, kod semafora, preko reke. They state a position and keep the same case with a verb of motion.
A masculine adjective has a short form for a first mention and a long form in -i for something already identified: nov most, novi most. An adjective inside a fixed name always takes the long form.

phrases.e: The bridge is over the river
There is a crowd in the town centre
Turn right at the traffic light

tips.b: Many country names are adjectives in form and decline as adjectives: Hrvatska, u Hrvatskoj; Nemačka, u Nemačkoj; Engleska, u Engleskoj. Names ending in -a decline as ordinary feminine nouns: Srbija, u Srbiji.
A language is named with the adjective in its bare masculine form and no separate word for language: srpski, engleski, nemački. Nationalities are separate nouns: Srbin, Srpkinja.

phrases.e: What language do you speak at home?

tips.b: The past is the short present of biti with the participle in -o, -la or -lo, which agrees in gender and number with the subject: radio sam, radila sam, radili smo.
The future is the short form ću, ćeš, će, ćemo, ćete, će with the infinitive. When the verb stands first the two fuse into one word: radiću, doći ću.
Voleti covers both liking and loving and takes the accusative. Moći is followed by da with a present form, or by a bare infinitive.
